planting.note: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; haritaki is a frost-tender tropical and subtropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.

directions: Plant grafted or seedling trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; haritaki is a frost-tender tropical and subtropical tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. One of the most revered trees in Ayurvedic medicine, called the 'king of medicines,' it is a deciduous forest tree native from India to Southeast Asia bearing small, ribbed, olive-like fruit that is dried and used as one of the three fruits in the classic Ayurvedic formula triphala, valued in traditional practice for digestive support among many other uses. The tree needs many years of growth before fruiting begins and ultimately becomes a substantial shade tree, making it a long-term planting suited only to large tropical properties, botanical collections, or dedicated medicinal orchards rather than a typical home garden. Water regularly while young, reduce watering once established, and expect a long wait before the first harvestable fruit crop.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring alongside a compatible host plant (sandalwood is a partial root parasite and needs a nearby host tree or shrub to thrive) in well-drained soil in full sun; realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring alongside a compatible host plant (sandalwood is a partial root parasite and needs a nearby host tree or shrub to thrive) in well-drained soil in full sun; realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. This slow-growing tropical tree produces the fragrant, dense, oil-rich heartwood prized for centuries in incense, perfumery, and religious ceremonies across South and Southeast Asia, but the tree must be interplanted with a suitable host species from an early age, since its roots form haustoria that tap into a neighboring plant's roots for water and nutrients even as it also photosynthesizes on its own. Decades of growth (typically fifteen years or more) are needed before the valuable, densely aromatic heartwood develops in commercially useful quantity, making it a long-term, multi-generational planting rather than a quick garden project, and wild populations have historically been overharvested, making legally sourced plantation-grown seedlings the responsible choice. Water young trees regularly during establishment, choose a nitrogen-fixing or otherwise compatible host species to plant alongside it, and be prepared for a very long wait before any wood harvest.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden
CSIRO (Australia) Sandalwood Research

planting.note: Plant seedlings or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, extremely well-drained, rocky soil in full sun; Indian frankincense is a dryland tree that needs sharp drainage above all else and is realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11.

directions: Plant seedlings or rooted cuttings in spring in lean, extremely well-drained, rocky soil in full sun; Indian frankincense is a dryland tree that needs sharp drainage above all else and is realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11. Native to dry, rocky hills across India, it is tapped for its fragrant resin, which hardens into aromatic amber 'tears' burned as incense and used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine, closely related to the African and Arabian frankincense trees that supply the resin of biblical and ancient trade fame. The papery, peeling bark and sparse, compound leaves give the tree an open, drought-adapted silhouette suited to a xeriscape or succulent-collection planting in frost-free climates, where it can be grown as much for its unusual form as for eventual resin tapping. Water sparingly, provide maximum sun and heat, and avoid any risk of standing water at the roots, which quickly kills this dryland species.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; forskohlii is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11.

directions: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; forskohlii is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. A relative of ornamental coleus and culinary sage, this fleshy-rooted perennial produces soft, aromatic, gray-green leaves and small blue-purple flowers, but is grown chiefly for its thick, tuberous roots, the source of the compound forskolin studied in traditional Ayurvedic medicine and modern dietary supplements. It tolerates poor, dry, sandy soil and drought better than ornamental coleus relatives, reflecting its native habitat on dry, rocky hillsides in India, and is easy to propagate from stem cuttings or root divisions. Harvest roots for use after the plant has grown for at least one full season, and protect from any frost, since both foliage and roots are damaged by freezing temperatures.

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Indian snakeroot is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Wild populations are heavily overharvested and vulnerable across much of its native range, so source only nursery-propagated plants.

directions: Plant transplants after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Indian snakeroot is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11. Wild populations are heavily overharvested and vulnerable across much of its native range, so source only nursery-propagated plants. Glossy, whorled leaves and small clusters of white flowers followed by small purple-black fruit grow on a compact forest-understory shrub native to South and Southeast Asian shade, historically significant as the original plant source of reserpine, one of the first modern drugs used to treat high blood pressure, and long used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine before that. Because unsustainable wild collection has made the species vulnerable across parts of its range, cultivated plantings from nursery-propagated stock, whether in a botanical collection or a home shade garden in a frost-free climate, help take pressure off remaining wild populations. Provide consistent warmth, humidity, and shade, and never attempt to self-medicate with plant material, since reserpine and related alkaloids have a narrow margin of safety and require professional medical guidance.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health reference
IUCN Red List reference

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining stems; Indian sarsaparilla is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11.

directions: Plant transplants after last frost in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade near a support for the twining stems; Indian sarsaparilla is frost-tender and grown as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 9-11. Slender, twining stems carry narrow, leathery leaves with a whitish midrib and small, purplish-brown flowers, but the plant is grown chiefly for its long, aromatic, cinnamon-scented roots, traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine and as a flavoring agent similar to true sarsaparilla, to which it is not closely related botanically. It tolerates a range of soil conditions and light levels once established, scrambling over low supports or trailing from a container, and roots are typically harvested for use after at least a year or two of growth. Water moderately, allowing soil to dry somewhat between waterings, and protect from any frost, which damages both foliage and roots.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; shankhpushpi is a low, spreading groundcover that tolerates poor, dry soil and needs minimal supplemental water once established.

directions: Direct sow or plant transplants after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; shankhpushpi is a low, spreading groundcover that tolerates poor, dry soil and needs minimal supplemental water once established. Small, hairy, gray-green leaves and delicate, pale blue to white, funnel-shaped morning-glory-like flowers cover a low, sprawling groundcover native to dry open ground across India, harvested whole (leaves, stems, and flowers together) for use in traditional Ayurvedic preparations valued for their calming properties. Its low, spreading habit and drought tolerance make it a workable, unfussy groundcover for a warm-climate medicinal or ethnobotanical garden bed, tolerating heat and poor soil with little care once established. Harvest above-ground growth as needed through the growing season, and expect the plant to die back in any significant cold, behaving as a tender perennial in the warmest zones or an annual further north.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
